newsitem.title: GERMANY: Duisenberg officially joins Euro central bank race.
newsitem.headline: Duisenberg officially joins Euro central bank race.

text.p: Dutch central bank chief Wim Duisenberg officially threw his hat into the ring on Tuesday to become head of the future European Central Bank overseeing the new single currency.
Duisenberg also sought to establish his credentials as a moderate who could help to resolve disputes between European Union nations aiming for monetary union.

Duisenberg, slated to become president of the European Monetary Institute this summer and rumoured to be on the shortlist for president of the European Central Bank (ECB), officially declared his candidacy to German newspapers on Tuesday.
"I can make no secret of it, I am a candidate," the Boersen Zeitung quoted Duisenberg as saying, adding that he would be available for an entire first term of eight years.
The ECB will evolve from the European Monetary Institute in 1999 after nations adopt the single currency, the euro.
Duisenberg signalled moderation, which may be instrumental in tackling thorny political disputes, including his own candidacy for the job.

The German Bundesbank has indicated it favours Duisenberg. But France recently ruffled diplomatic feathers by intimating that Germany had earlier agreed to support a French candidate in return for siting the central bank in Frankfurt.
Duisenberg stressed that no political agreements had been reached between France and Germany, and that the race to head the ECB was still on.
In an interview with Die Welt, he took a middle road on a French proposal for a stability council which would act as a counterweight to the planned ECB, and for regular government consultations.

"According to my information, (the French proposals) refer to the setting up of informal meetings by finance ministers participating in the euro. That in itself is a perfectly normal thing. It is also possible under the Maastricht Treaty."

But he added the European Union did not need more formal institutions, noting that the French had in the meantime denied they were seeking formal meetings of a body to act as a counterweight to the ECB.
"The ECB's main priority is to guarantee price stability," he said.
Duisenberg's standing in Germany has risen as he comes from a country familiar with stability policies and he supports them for Europe.
Duisenberg said that the three Benelux countries plus Germany, France, Austria, Finland and Ireland were likely to join currency union at the scheduled starting date on January 1, 1999.
Other countries were making impressive efforts to meet the criteria for joining but it remained open whether they would make it in time.

"But it's not a catastrophe if one, two, three, four countries join a little later," he said, adding that he expected all 15 nations to have joined by the time the new currency was circulated in 2002.

Duisenberg took a strict stance on the entry criteria for monetary union, saying it was not enough for countries to get their budget deficits in shape just for 1997. Medium-term budget prospects needed to be assessed.
Duisenberg said he had "no problems" with the dollar's recent sharp rise to around 1.64 marks.
Much more important was the fundamental stability of exchange rates, and expectations for exchange rates to remain stable, he stressed.
Industry, in particular, needed an assurance that exchange rates between the dollar, the mark, the franc and other units remained stable, he added.
There was also no reason to suspect that intra-European squabbling on monetary union issues had triggered the dollar's moves, Duisenberg said.
